0.text: People with imposter syndrome often underestimate their abilities and attribute their success to external factors, such as luck or help from others, instead of recognizing their own skills and efforts.
0.fact: Emma Watson, the well-known actress and activist, has spoken openly about her feelings of being an imposter. Despite her success in film and activism, she has often doubted her abilities and feared that people would discover she was “inadequate.”

1.text: Feeling like you come across as more competent than you believe yourself to be is a hallmark of imposter syndrome. People with this syndrome often feel their success is undeserved and fear being “found out.”
1.fact: According to the American Psychological Association, about 25% of office workers feel less competent than their colleagues believe them to be.

2.text: Fear of being evaluated is a common symptom of imposter syndrome. People with this syndrome often worry that their work won’t be good enough.
2.fact: Fear of evaluation can lead to procrastination and the avoidance of tasks that require review and feedback. This reinforces feelings of insecurity and self-criticism.

3.text: Accepting praise and acknowledging your achievements are important steps in overcoming imposter syndrome. Psychologists recommend regularly reminding yourself of your successes and merits, as well as learning to accept compliments without internal resistance.
3.fact: In a survey of students at prestigious universities, about 60% admitted to feeling less confident in their abilities after receiving positive feedback or praise.

4.text: Recognizing your skills and hard work is a vital step toward overcoming imposter syndrome. People who regularly analyze and acknowledge their successes are less likely to experience imposter feelings.
4.fact: Tina Fey, the renowned comedian and writer, has frequently mentioned her feelings of being an imposter. She often felt her success in comedy and television was accidental. In her book “Bossypants,” she shares her doubts and fears, showing that even the most successful people can feel like they don’t belong.

5.text: Psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), helps people recognize and change their negative thoughts and beliefs. CBT helps develop a more realistic perception of one’s abilities and achievements.
5.fact: Tom Hanks, the famous actor and two-time Oscar winner, has spoken candidly about his fear of being exposed. He admitted that he often feels like an imposter and fears people will realize he isn’t as talented as they think.

6.text: People with imposter syndrome often focus on their failures while ignoring or downplaying their successes. This phenomenon is linked to cognitive distortions, such as a mental filter and discounting the positive.
6.fact: Michelle Obama, the former First Lady of the United States, has spoken about her feelings of being an imposter and her tendency to focus on failures. In her memoir “Becoming,” she shares how she had to struggle with the feeling that her successes were accidental and undeserved, and how she learned to acknowledge and value her achievements.

7.text: Feeling dissatisfied with work results and striving for perfection are common symptoms of imposter syndrome. People with this syndrome often set unrealistically high standards for themselves, leading to a constant sense that their work is never good enough.
7.fact: The drive for perfectionism can intensify feelings of being an imposter. People who constantly strive for perfection often experience anxiety and a fear of failure, which hinders them from acknowledging their achievements.

8.text: This cognitive distortion is often called the “illusion of randomness” and is linked to low self-esteem and high levels of self-criticism. People with this distortion often underestimate their abilities and believe their success is unearned.
8.fact: Albert Einstein, one of the greatest scientists of all time, often spoke about his feelings of being an imposter. Despite his extraordinary scientific achievements, he believed his success was accidental and a result of luck. Einstein once said, “I feel a sense of injustice toward those who overestimate my abilities and achievements.”

9.text: Negative thoughts and an inner critic can undermine the ability to accept positive feedback. People with imposter syndrome often interpret compliments as exaggerated or undeserved, which prevents them from owning their successes.
9.fact: According to surveys, about 60% of women and 40% of men report that they find it difficult to accept compliments in professional settings because they feel unworthy.

10.text: People with imposter syndrome often feel that their success is due to luck or chance rather than their own abilities. This can lead to constant anxiety and the fear of being exposed.
10.fact: External success and recognition do not always eliminate imposter feelings. Even people who have reached the heights of their professions may continue to feel like “frauds.”

11.text: Negative thoughts and an inner critic can undermine the ability to accept positive feedback. People with imposter syndrome often interpret compliments as exaggerated or undeserved, which prevents them from owning their successes.
11.fact: According to surveys, about 60% of women and 40% of men report that they find it difficult to accept compliments in professional settings because they feel unworthy.

12.text: People with imposter syndrome often possess high levels of intelligence and competence, but their internal beliefs do not align with reality. They may underestimate their abilities and achievements, leading to constant feelings of anxiety.
12.fact: Practicing positive self-talk and self-acceptance can help reduce the fear of being exposed. Psychotherapists recommend keeping track of your successes and recognition to remind yourself of your competence.

13.text: Fear of failure, even after successfully completing similar tasks in the past, is a characteristic manifestation of imposter syndrome. This fear can limit professional growth and personal development, as the individual avoids new challenges and opportunities.
13.fact: Fear of failure is often linked to perfectionism and high expectations. People with imposter syndrome may set unrealistically high standards for themselves, which intensifies their fear of failure.

14.text: Doubting one’s ability to repeat success, despite recognition, can arise from cognitive distortions such as “imposter phenomenon” and the “paradox of superiority.” People experiencing these distortions tend to downplay their successes and view them as accidental.
14.fact: These doubts may be related to the Dunning-Kruger effect, where highly skilled people underestimate their abilities, while less competent people overestimate their skills. People with imposter syndrome often fall into the first group.

15.text: The tendency to discount one’s achievements, despite praise and recognition, is linked to a cognitive distortion known as “discounting the positive.” People with this distortion tend to ignore or minimize the significance of their successes and achievements.
15.fact: Psychologists recommend practicing mindful recognition of your successes and achievements. This can be done by keeping a gratitude journal to record positive moments and achievements, or by discussing your successes with trusted people.

16.text: Constantly comparing yourself to others can lead to a “scarcity effect,” where a person focuses on their flaws and underestimates their strengths and achievements.
16.fact: People struggling with imposter syndrome often forget that others may also experience similar doubts and insecurities. Realizing this can help reduce feelings of loneliness and inadequacy.

17.text: Anxiety before tasks is often linked to perfectionism and fear of failure. People with imposter syndrome may set unrealistically high standards for themselves, which increases their worry.
17.fact: Research shows that positive reinforcement and support from others can significantly reduce anxiety levels and increase confidence. Developing self-support and mindfulness skills also helps in managing imposter syndrome.

18.text: Surveys among professionals show that about 55% of respondents delay talking about their successes, fearing they might not happen or might be perceived negatively.
18.fact: Sheryl Sandberg, former COO of Facebook and author of “Lean In,” admitted that she often felt afraid to share her successes and achievements. She feared that if she shared them too early, she wouldn’t be able to live up to expectations or would face criticism.

19.text: The drive to be the best can lead to burnout and chronic stress. People experiencing imposter syndrome often work harder and longer to meet their high standards, which negatively impacts their mental and physical health.
19.fact: Serena Williams, one of the most successful tennis players of all time, has spoken about her drive to be the best and her feelings of being an imposter. Despite her numerous victories and achievements, she often felt the pressure to always be at the top and the fear of not meeting expectations.

normal.text: Your results indicate a steady sense of competence and self-confidence. You don’t tend to excessively doubt your achievements or compare yourself to others, and you’re able to openly acknowledge your successes. Even when facing mistakes, you maintain confidence in your abilities and keep moving forward. This mature attitude toward yourself helps you grow and provides a sense of inner stability.
normal.title: Confidence in your own value

light.text: Sometimes you may find it difficult to fully embrace your achievements or accept praise calmly, without feeling internal tension. At times, you might compare yourself to others or doubt whether you’re meeting expectations. However, overall, you’re able to return to an objective view, acknowledge your efforts, and see your strengths. This is a good foundation for further building your self-confidence.
light.title: Mild signs of imposter syndrome

severe.text: Your results show that feelings of doubt regarding your own competence may significantly affect your confidence and your ability to express yourself freely. You might often feel a fear of “not measuring up” or worry that others will notice your weaknesses. This inner critic can prevent you from truly owning your achievements and reaching your full potential. Seeking support, working on self-esteem, and practicing self-compassion can help ease this pressure.
severe.title: Strong signs of imposter syndrome

extreme.text: Your results indicate a strong internal vulnerability toward acknowledging your achievements. You may often feel that your successes are just luck, while mistakes are seen as proof of inadequacy. This state can be emotionally exhausting and can prevent you from feeling satisfied with your journey. Remember: you don’t have to handle this alone—seeking support and working with your inner critic can be a vital step toward confidence and self-acceptance.
extreme.title: Pronounced signs of imposter syndrome

text: Have you ever had moments where success felt like a fluke and your own achievements felt undeserved?
Imposter syndrome is an emotional state where it is difficult for a person to acknowledge their competence and merits, even when they are obvious to others.
This test will help you assess how much this state affects your life and will serve as a first step toward a deeper understanding of yourself and your strengths.
